summary: EarthFM is an interactive tool designed to allow you to not only see the trends and data of various Earth data types, but hear and compare them among others. By leveraging an algorithmically generated song generation, we are able to consistently and definitively see trends in the data and allow people of all abilities to understand our beautiful Earth. Additionally, we incorporated a "game" that allows people to build intuition about the data they are hearing, learn about the reason why these trends happen, and maybe even predict the future! Finally, by incorporating many accessibility options, such as captions and voice capability (for both reading and writing text), we ensure that everyone is able to love the Earth we are in.
details:
The problem
NASA’s Earth Information Center shows the planet changing through some of the most striking visualizations NASA makes: warming oceans, spreading wildfires, a heating planet. But every one of them is a color map. If you’re blind, low vision, or colorblind, you can’t read them. That’s 43 million people who are blind and 295 million more with moderate or severe vision loss (The Lancet Global Health, 2021). Public data isn’t the same as accessible data.

What we built
EarthFM is a jukebox for the planet: a free web app where every place on Earth has a song, and every note is NASA data. Click any spot on the world map, or explore it by keyboard, and EarthFM plays that place’s data as music, generated live in the browser.

Three NASA data layers, each with its own song

  • Sea heat: ocean surface temperature from NASA’s ocean model (SVS 3912). Higher notes mean warmer water.
  • Wildfires: active fires detected by the VIIRS satellite instruments (SVS 5113). More notes mean more fire.
  • Global heat: surface temperature change compared with the 1951 to 1980 average, from NASA GISTEMP (SVS 5207). Higher notes mean hotter than normal.

How we turn pictures back into data
EarthFM doesn’t “listen” to how an image looks. It reads the science inside it. Our Python pipeline downloads each NASA frame and matches every pixel’s color to that visualization’s official color bar to recover the real value. For sea heat, that’s blue at 0 °C up to red at 32 °C. For global heat, it’s blue at −2 °C through white to red at +2 °C. We average those values onto a 10° grid of the whole globe, for every date in the series. That gives us a global timeline of real numbers, and the music plays those numbers.

How data becomes music

  • Pitch = value. Every place uses the same fixed pitch range for a layer, so you can compare two places by ear. A warmer ocean literally sounds higher.
  • Silence = no data. A square with no ocean plays nothing, so in the sea heat layer you can hear coastlines as gaps in the music.
    • By Area sweeps across the region around your place on one date, left to right, with each note panned to where it sits on the map. You hear the shape of the data in space.
    • By Time follows your place’s average through every date: notes rise and fall with the trend, and the rhythm speeds up when the picture is changing fast. You hear change unfold over time.
  • Same value, same sound, every time. The music is fully driven by the data, so what you hear is something you can trust.

Features

  • Jukebox map: click anywhere to add a place, drag a place to move it, or type a name in the search box.
  • Mixtapes: string places into a route and fly between them song by song, with a plane on the map. Share the whole mixtape with one link.
  • “How this sound is made” panel: for every song, shows the NASA picture it came from, how the colors were read, what the notes and silences mean, and the data’s honest limits. For example, the wildfire layer measures fire visible in NASA’s image, not the area burned.
  • Game mode: three rounds built on NASA EIC data: Lights On (night lights, SVS 5313), Rising Seas (sea level, SVS 5235) and Arctic Heat (GISTEMP, SVS 5207). You hear reference sounds, then a mystery sound, and guess what it represents. It trains your ear to read data.

Built for every listener
Accessibility isn’t an add-on in EarthFM. It’s the reason EarthFM exists.

  • Voice guidance reads what’s playing using the browser’s built-in speech, and turns the music down while it talks so you never miss either.
  • Explore by ear: hold Shift and use the arrow keys to move across the globe as it announces each place. Press Enter to add one.
  • Spoken commands: H reads every shortcut aloud; W says what’s playing; L lists your mixtape; R repeats the last description.
  • Live captions for every song, for Deaf and hard of hearing users. Captions and voice always say the same thing.
  • Mono audio for people who hear with one ear, full keyboard control, screen reader support, and support for reduced motion and high contrast.

Why it matters
NASA has already shown that people learn through sound: in a study of 3,184 sighted and blind or low vision participants, NASA’s sonifications of space data produced significant self-reported learning gains (Arcand et al., 2024). But those projects sonified distant galaxies. EarthFM brings the same idea home, to the climate data about the planet we actually live on, and lets people explore it interactively instead of just listening. It turns NASA’s open data into something anyone can use, whether they see it, hear it, or both.

What’s next

  • A live exhibit at NASA’s Earth Information Center
  • Classroom use, where visually impaired and sighted students learn side by side
  • Spatial audio with head tracking, so you can turn toward a wildfire and hear it get louder
  • More NASA datasets, from sea ice to Mars
  • Co-design and testing with blind and low vision listeners

Built with
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tone.js (live audio synthesis), the Web Speech API (voice), Python (the data pipeline), Figma (design).
dataRefs: SVS 3912: Sea surface temperature (Sea heat layer)
SVS 5207: GISTEMP surface temperature change (Global heat layer and the Arctic Heat game round)
SVS 5313: Change in Night Lights, 2012 to 2023 (Lights On game round)
SVS 5235: Sea Level Through a Porthole, EIC Climate Vital Signs (Rising Seas game round)
